label: bm-safety-lca
topic: Safety, toxicology and sustainability of the printed resins (Formlabs Form 4 SLA resins and Fuse 1+ SLS powders): skin contact, VOC, leaching, handling, IPA washing, disposal, recyclability, life cycle, honest bio-based and sustainability claims
summary: SAFETY. All 14 Formlabs SLA resins whose safety data sheets I read (18 sheets, 15 resin files) are skin sensitisers as liquids (H317). Rigid 10K and Silicone 40A carry only that class. Flexible 80A V2 and High Temp V2 cause serious eye damage (H318), and Durable V2 and High Temp V2 are classified reproductive toxicants 1B (H360), ingredient not disclosed. Flexible 50A's EU sheet adds H411 (aquatic) that its US sheet omits. The resins are not flammable (flash point above 93.5 C); the wash solvent isopropanol is (flash point 12 C, H225). Formlabs prescribes nitrile or neoprene gloves, glasses, three air changes per hour, and resin-specific wash times (Flexible 50A at most 20 min since longer 'may degrade parts', and it takes up 39 % IPA in 24 h; Silicone 40A needs an 80/20 IPA to n-butyl acetate bath in a dedicated bucket). Independent chamber studies find SLA printing, washing and curing emit 30 to over 100 VOCs (over 4 mg/h), idle open vats emit as much as printing (a lid cuts it 70-97 %), and cured parts keep outgassing, falling 84-96 % over 28 days. An SLA plastic leached photoinitiator at up to 200 mg/L into water in 24 h and the extract killed zebrafish embryos, which matters for any water-cycled hygromorph. Nylon powders are only combustible dust; SLS needs a grounded vacuum, humidity under 50 %, and an oxygen alarm if nitrogen is used. DISPOSAL. Liquid resin goes to a chemical waste stream (or is cured in sunlight 1-10 days), used IPA to a waste service, cured parts to household waste. RECYCLING AND LCA. Formlabs says cured resin, sintered powder and parts cannot be recycled; 30-50 % refresh means 50-70 % of the unfused Nylon 11 is reused in the next build, which is reuse, not recycling. No Formlabs life-cycle assessment was found; a PA12 recycling LCA ranges from 26 % lower to 68 % higher global warming potential than PA66 depending on allocation. BIO-BASED. Formlabs calls Nylon 11 'bio-based' with no percentage; 100 % bio-based carbon is Arkema's figure for its own grade. No resin is bio-based. EU Directive 2024/825 names 'biobased' as a generic claim to be avoided from 27 Sept 2026. VERSUS EARLIER AGENTS: confirms the Nylon 11 bio-based finding and the 39 % IPA uptake; deepens them. No earlier claim contradicted. Two data-hygiene flags: MANIFEST maps flexible50a_ENUS__2379.pdf to a URL that says Flexible-80A-Resin-V2 though the file is Flexible 50A, and 'Elastic 50A V2' is now named Flexible 50A.
lay_summary: Printing liquid resin is a bit like handling a very strong glue: touching it again and again can give you a lasting allergy, so you wear nitrile gloves and goggles. The cleaning bath of isopropyl alcohol is the part that can catch fire, so it must be kept away from sparks. Once the plastic is washed and baked hard, it is much safer, but studies show it still gives off tiny amounts of fumes for about four weeks, and unreacted chemicals can wash out into water. Formlabs itself says the hardened parts and the used powder cannot be recycled, so they go in the bin. The nylon 11 powder is described as bio-based, but nobody has published how much, so an architect should never say it is green, recyclable or biodegradable. The honest sentence is narrow and sourced, like: made from a powder the maker calls bio-based, with the percentage unknown.

findings.claim: Every one of the 14 distinct Formlabs SLA resin products whose safety data sheet (SDS) I read is classified as a skin sensitiser (H317, may cause an allergic skin reaction). Own tally over 15 SDS files (Flexible 50A has two) in sds_table.json, script sds_extract.py + calc.py.
findings.evidence_quote: H317 May cause an allergic skin reaction

findings.claim: Rigid 10K and Silicone 40A are the only two of the 14 resins whose SDS classification is H317 alone (no skin-irritation, eye-irritation or respiratory-irritation class). All other resins also carry H315 and/or H319 and/or H335, and two carry H318 or H360.
findings.evidence_quote: H317 May cause an allergic skin reaction

findings.claim: Flexible 80A V2 is classified 'Serious eye damage, category 1' (H318), the strongest eye class among the SLA resins read (shared only with High Temp V2). Eye protection (goggles) is therefore not optional when pouring or wiping this resin, which is the proposed swelling layer in the project.
findings.value: H318 on Flexible 80A V2 and High Temp V2
findings.evidence_quote: Serious eye damage, category 1

findings.claim: High Temp V2 resin is classified reproductive toxicity category 1B (H360, may impair fertility and the fetus), signal word Danger. The SDS does not name which ingredient causes it (section 3 lists 'Acrylated Monomer(s)' etc. as Trade Secret).
findings.evidence_quote: H360 May impair fertility. May impair fetus.

findings.claim: Durable V2/V2.1 resin is likewise classified Repr. 1B (H360, may damage fertility or the unborn child), plus H411 (toxic to aquatic life with long-lasting effects). Ingredient not named in the SDS.
findings.evidence_quote: H360 May damage fertility or the unborn child.

findings.claim: The EU (CLP) SDS for Flexible 50A, dated 2026-05-29, carries H411 (chronic aquatic hazard category 2); the US (HazCom) SDS of the same product and date does not. Same product, different regional label: a European client or studio must use the EU sheet. The US file is named flexible50a_ENUS in the earlier MANIFEST but its URL says Flexible-80A-Resin-V2; its content is Flexible 50A.
findings.evidence_quote: H411 Toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects

findings.claim: Flexible 50A US SDS lists 'Methacrylate Ester Monomer' at 70-90 % by weight and a photoinitiator that the EU SDS identifies as BAPO (<2 %, Skin Sens. 1A, Aquatic Chronic 4). So the soft, high-swelling resin is mostly a single monomer class.
findings.evidence_quote: Methacrylate Ester Monomer

findings.claim: As supplied, the resins are not flammable by SDS (flash point above 93.5 C), so the fire risk in a resin room comes from the wash solvent, not the resin. Rigid 10K SDS section 9.
findings.evidence_quote: Flammability Not Flammable

findings.claim: Acute oral and dermal toxicity of the Rigid 10K ingredients is low (rat oral LD50 >5000 mg/kg and dermal >2000 mg/kg for urethane dimethacrylate), so the dominant risk is allergy, not poisoning.
findings.value: UDMA oral LD50 >5000 mg/kg; dermal >2000 mg/kg
findings.evidence_quote: Urethane Dimethacrylate oral LD50 Rat: >5000 mg/kg

findings.claim: Rigid 10K is described by Formlabs as 'highly glass-filled' but its SDS section 3 itemises only urethane dimethacrylate 15-25 %, methacrylate monomer 7-10 % and photoinitiator <0.5 %. By my arithmetic 64.5 to 78 % of the mass is not itemised (probably the glass; that attribution is my inference). Sanding or machining cured Rigid 10K therefore makes glass-filled dust that the SDS does not describe.
findings.evidence_quote: This highly glass-filled resin is the stiffest material in our engineering portfolio.

findings.claim: Formlabs says sensitisation is cumulative and lasting, which is why a 'non-irritant' label does not remove the need for gloves.
findings.evidence_quote: irritation is dose-dependent and reversible, while sensitization is cumulative and, once established, lasting.

findings.claim: Formlabs recommends nitrile or neoprene gloves for liquid resin and wash solvent, safety glasses, and respiratory protection only if exposure limits are exceeded or ventilation is poor.
findings.evidence_quote: Always wear non-reactive nitrile or neoprene gloves to prevent skin contact with liquid resin and wash solvents.

findings.claim: An independent 1992 glove study found no permeation of two multifunctional acrylates (HDDA, TMPTA) and two HDDA/EHA mixtures through nitrile or butyl rubber at 20 C, but permeation of HDDA through natural rubber with breakthrough in 30-60 min. It did not test the actual Formlabs mixtures or monofunctional methacrylates, so it supports 'nitrile, not natural rubber' but not a breakthrough time for Formlabs resin.
findings.value: nitrile: no permeation of tested acrylates; natural rubber: 30-60 min
findings.evidence_quote: None of the acrylate compounds nor mixtures was found to permeate the butyl or nitrile rubber under the test conditions.

findings.claim: Formlabs states its resins do not require a respirator, yet 8 of the 14 SDS carry H335 (may cause respiratory irritation). Both statements come from Formlabs; they are reconcilable only because the SDS asks for ventilation and a respirator 'if engineering controls do not maintain airborne concentrations below limits'.
findings.value: H335 on 8 of 14; FAQ says no respirator needed
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs resins do not require a respirator.

findings.claim: Formlabs asserts that its resins contain no ACMO (N-acryloylmorpholine), a monomer it flags as a serious eye and organ hazard. The SDS compositions are mostly 'Trade Secret', so this cannot be independently confirmed from public documents.
findings.evidence_quote: Alpha Resins and other Formlabs resins do not contain ACMO.

findings.claim: Formlabs says acrylic monomers are 'inert once fully polymerized' and that an incompletely cured part can still cause a reaction. Independent work (next findings) shows cured parts still outgas for weeks and can leach unreacted photoinitiator, so 'inert' is an overstatement and 'safe to handle' depends on the wash and cure workflow.
findings.evidence_quote: acrylic monomers are contact allergens in liquid form but inert once fully polymerized, so an incompletely cured part can still cause a reaction.

findings.claim: Silicone 40A is the only elastomer resin read with a published skin-contact test: evaluated as a skin contacting device under ISO 10993-1, not cytotoxic (-5), not an irritant (-23), not a sensitizer (-10), tested at NAMSA. Tough 1500 V2 has the same three results, but only for parts washed 10 min, dried at least 30 min and post-cured at 70 C for 12 min.
findings.evidence_quote: Silicone 40A Resin has been evaluated as a skin contacting device in accordance with ISO 10993-1, and passed the requirements

findings.claim: The Tough 1500 V2 skin-contact result applies to a defined workflow: 'washed in a Form Wash for 10 minutes' then dried and 'post-cured at 70 C for 12 minutes in a Form Cure'. A different wash, sanding, water cycling or a different cure is outside what was tested.
findings.value: result valid for stated workflow only
findings.evidence_quote: washed in a Form Wash for 10 minutes (5 min

findings.claim: The technical data sheets for Rigid 10K, Flexible 80A V2 and Flexible 50A (versions read) contain no ISO 10993 or biocompatibility statement. I found no skin-contact claim for them; absence confirmed by grep of the saved TDS text, not by a quote.
findings.value: no biocompatibility claim for Rigid 10K, Flexible 80A V2, Flexible 50A

findings.claim: A 2025 scoping review (J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol) finds resin-printer VOCs reported mostly as carbonyl compounds or methacrylate monomers, that specific VOCs measured fell below British workplace limits, but warns the methods differ from regulatory ones and that total VOC, long print times, several printers and poor ventilation raise exposure.
findings.value: VOCs mostly carbonyls and methacrylates; below WELs; caution
findings.evidence_quote: VOC emissions from resin 3D printers have been reported mostly as carbonyl compounds or methacrylate monomers.

findings.claim: In one study cited by that review, a resin printer released isopropanol at 560 ppbV; against the 400 ppmV limit quoted there that is 0.14 % (own calculation: 560e-9/400e-6 = 0.0014). Measured single-compound levels are low; the open question is the mixture and the sensitising monomers.
findings.evidence_quote: The isopropanol emissions were 560 ppbV (0.560 ppmV) compared to the occupational TWA exposure limit of 400 ppmV

findings.claim: The same review reports a chamber study on a Formlabs Form 2 with clear and castable-wax resin: clear resin emitted 2-hydroxypropyl methacrylate, ethyl methacrylate and methyl methacrylate at about 4-6 ug/m3, ingredients listed in the SDS only as 'unspecified methacrylate monomers'. Form 2 is an older printer than the Form 4.
findings.evidence_quote: The most abundant VOCs for the clear resin were 2-hydroxypropyl methacrylate (6 µg/m 3 ), ethyl methacrylate (4 µg/m 3 ) and methyl methacrylate (6 µg/m 3 )

findings.claim: A 2022 chamber study of SLA printing plus wash and cure units found 30 to over 100 VOCs per phase, total VOC above typical filament-printer levels (over 4 mg/h), and estimated personal exposure to formaldehyde and naphthalene above California OEHHA recommended indoor levels. This disagrees in emphasis with the 'below workplace limits' reading of the scoping review: both are true because one compares to workplace limits and the other to stricter indoor-air guidelines.
findings.value: TVOC >4 mg/h; formaldehyde, naphthalene above OEHHA levels
findings.evidence_quote: The total VOC emissions from SLA processes were higher than typical levels from material extrusion 3D printing, and the emission rate could be over 4 mg/h.

findings.claim: A 2025 chamber study of two SLA printer brands found printer brand strongly influences SLA emissions (a built-in resin heater was part of the explanation), while resin colour mattered little. Emission numbers from one printer or the older Form 2 do not transfer to a Form 4.
findings.evidence_quote: Printer brand strongly influenced the emission yields.

findings.claim: A 2025 study found idle printers with an uncovered vat emitted as much as or more than active printing, and a fitted lid cut idle emissions by 70-97 %; a so-called 'Eco' resin emitted less than the standard one but both approached exposure thresholds. Practical rule: keep the vat covered, remove the resin tank only when needed.
findings.evidence_quote: idle printer emissions were reduced drastically (by 70–97%) using a fabricated vat lid

findings.claim: Cured resin parts keep emitting. A 2021 study measured outgassing of cured parts for 84 days: total emissions fell by 84-96 % over 28 days, from 3000-14000 to 100-1000 ug/m2/h, parts warmed to 37 C emitted 1.4-2.9 times more, and the authors suggest storing parts for 4 weeks before consumer use. Directly relevant to a pavilion or interior installation.
findings.evidence_quote: Manufactured resin products are suggested to be stored for 4 weeks after their production to reduce potential consumer VOC hazards.

findings.claim: The same study identified sensitising acrylates and carcinogenic formaldehyde among emitted compounds, and average VOC concentration at the printer of only 41-87 ug/m3: low, but not zero hazard.
findings.evidence_quote: The identified compounds included hazardous species included sensitizing acrylates and carcinogenic formaldehyde.

findings.claim: Formlabs' air-quality position: all its facilities remain below OSHA limits, but 'air quality results are specific to Formlabs facilities and are not transferable to other locations'. A studio needs its own assessment; Formlabs recommends rooms with at least three full air exchanges per hour.
findings.value: >=3 air changes per hour; results not transferable
findings.evidence_quote: Air quality results are specific to Formlabs facilities and are not transferable to other locations.

findings.claim: Formlabs recommends SLA products be used in a room with at least three full air exchanges per hour (HVAC), not in closets or small unventilated storage rooms.
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs recommends using its SLA products in room equipped with HVAC systems providing at least three full air exchanges per hour.

findings.claim: Formlabs' UL GREENGUARD Gold certification applies only to its Alpha resins printed on Form Studio 1 with the VOC Extractor, and Formlabs itself says it is for the printing process, not just the final part. It must not be quoted for Form 4 resins, Flexible, Rigid or Silicone, or for finished parts.
findings.value: GREENGUARD Gold: Alpha resins on Form Studio 1 only
findings.evidence_quote: This certification is for the printing process - not just for a final part.

findings.claim: Sanding cured parts: Formlabs advises respiratory protection (N95 or better) and wet sanding to limit dust.
findings.evidence_quote: You may also want to wear respiratory protection when sanding your printed parts. You can also wet sand to minimize dust.

findings.claim: A 2025 feeding study with sanded SLA resin particles in house crickets found changed enzyme activities (digestive, antioxidative) but no statistically significant difference in mortality between dose groups, so the ecotoxicity of cured-resin sanding dust is unsettled; I rate it weak evidence either way.
findings.evidence_quote: There were no statistically significant differences between the groups in terms of mortality rate, according to the Kruskal–Wallis test, p > 0.05.

findings.claim: An SLA-printed plastic leached unreacted photoinitiator 1-hydroxycyclohexyl phenyl ketone into water at up to 200 mg/L in the first 24 h; the extract killed zebrafish embryos (LC50 22.25 % v/v). The abstract names an SLA process, not a Formlabs resin, so it shows the mechanism, not a Formlabs-specific number. Any water-cycling hygromorph facade will extract from its resin the same way.
findings.value: up to 200 mg/L in 24 h; LC50 22.25 % v/v
findings.evidence_quote: Migration of unpolymerized photoinitiator, 1-hydroxycyclohexyl phenyl ketone (1-HCHPK) from a plastic solid phase to aqueous media at up to 200 mg/L in the first 24 h was detected

findings.claim: Formlabs' own solvent-compatibility table shows some resins lose mass in some liquids (negative 24 h weight change), which means extraction can outweigh uptake. This is the earlier project record (spec-resin-chemistry.json) and I did not re-fetch the table.
findings.evidence_quote: Risk, leaching visible in Formlabs' own data: several resins show negative 24 h weight change in some liquids

findings.claim: IPA is the flammable item in a resin studio: Formlabs labels it 'Danger' and says use and store it away from ignition sources; PubChem lists a closed-cup flash point of 12 C (53 F) and GHS H225 (highly flammable liquid and vapour) for isopropanol, against >93.5 C for the resins themselves.
findings.value: IPA flash point 12 C closed cup; H225
findings.evidence_quote: 12 °C, 53 °F (Closed cup)

findings.claim: GHS classification of isopropanol on PubChem: H225 flammable, H319 eye irritation, H336 drowsiness or dizziness (narcotic effects). These apply to the wash bath, not the resin.
findings.evidence_quote: H225: Highly Flammable liquid and vapor [Danger Flammable liquids]

findings.claim: Formlabs wash bath maintenance: replace IPA when dissolved resin reaches 10 %; Form Wash V1 holds 8.6 L, V2 15 L and Form Wash L 42 L of solvent. Those volumes set the size of the flammable-liquid inventory and of the waste stream.
findings.evidence_quote: The Form Wash V1 holds 8.6 L of solvent. The Form Wash V2 holds 15 L of solvent. The Form Wash L holds 42 L of solvent.

findings.claim: Formlabs' danger notice on IPA: consult the supplier SDS first and keep IPA away from ignition sources.
findings.evidence_quote: IPA is flammable and should be used and stored away from ignition sources.

findings.claim: Wash time is resin-specific and too long is harmful to the part. Flexible 50A (formerly Elastic 50A V2): 20 min and 'avoid washing Elastic 50 A Resin for longer than 20 minutes, as this may degrade parts'. This ties to the project record that Elastic 50A V2 takes up 39.2 % IPA by mass in 24 h: the same bath that cleans the part swells it, extracts residues and leaves flammable solvent inside it.
findings.value: Flexible/Elastic 50A max 20 min; IPA uptake 39.2 % in 24 h
findings.evidence_quote: Avoid washing Elastic 50 A Resin for longer than 20 minutes, as this may degrade parts.

findings.claim: High Temp V2: wash 5 min, never more than 6 min total in solvent. Durable V2: 20 min and not longer than 20 min total. Both are the two H360 (reproductive toxicity 1B) resins, so short, controlled wash times also limit operator exposure.
findings.value: High Temp 5 (max 6) min; Durable 20 min max
findings.evidence_quote: Do not leave High Temp Resin in solvent for longer than 6 minutes total, as excessive solvent exposure affects the quality of the final part.

findings.claim: Rigid 10K is washed 10 + 10 min (second bath fresh) in its own bucket because it contains glass particles that otherwise stick to other resins' parts; Flexible 80A V2 is washed 5 + 5 min in two cycles with fresh solvent for the second.
findings.evidence_quote: Rigid 10K Resin contains glass particles, which strengthens printed parts. Maintain separate wash buckets to prevent glass particles adhering to parts printed with other resins.

findings.claim: Silicone 40A cannot be washed in plain IPA: Formlabs specifies an 80/20 IPA to n-butyl acetate mixture in a dedicated Form Wash bucket, or an IPA sonication procedure. n-Butyl acetate is a second flammable solvent and a different waste stream; plan for it before choosing Silicone 40A.
findings.evidence_quote: Do not wash with IPA alone unless following the instructions in the Silicone 40 A Resin IPA sonication wash guide .

findings.claim: Formlabs' non-flammable Resin Washing Solution is NOT recommended for Flexible 50A, Flexible 80A (V1, V2), Elastic 50A or Tough 1000, so the safer solvent is not available for the soft layers this project needs.
findings.value: Resin Washing Solution excluded for the elastomer resins
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs does not recommend using Resin Washing Solution to wash parts printed in this resin.

findings.claim: Dry before handling or curing: Formlabs recommends letting Tough 1000 parts air dry at least 30 minutes before handling or post-curing, and (castable resins) ensuring all solvent has evaporated before curing. Solvent-swollen elastomer parts should be dried at least as long.
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs recommends allowing parts printed in Tough 1000 Resin to air dry for at least 30 minutes prior to handling or post-curing.

findings.claim: Ventilate wash and dry areas: Formlabs says handle solvents with gloves in a well-ventilated area away from heat, sparks and flames, because IPA vapours are flammable.
findings.evidence_quote: Solvents such as isopropyl alcohol evaporate rapidly, and their vapors are flammable, so keep bottles closed whenever possible.

findings.claim: Liquid or partly cured resin may be hazardous waste: put it in the chemical waste stream; without one, Formlabs' fallback is to cure a small amount in a labelled container in sunlight for 1-10 days (405 nm light plus heat is faster), then bin the cured solid as household waste. Never down a drain.
findings.value: chemical waste stream, or cure 1-10 days in sunlight
findings.evidence_quote: Leave the container exposed to sunlight to cure for 1–10 days.

findings.claim: Regulatory status of liquid resin as waste depends on the region: Formlabs writes that liquid resin 'may be classified as hazardous waste in your region and shall be disposed of with care'. A UK or EU practice must check its local waste code; I did not find a single authoritative code.
findings.evidence_quote: Liquid resin (whether pure liquid, dissolved in solvent, or partially cured) may be classified as hazardous waste in your region and shall be disposed of with care.

findings.claim: Used IPA or TPM that contains dissolved resin must never go down a drain or into household waste; use a waste-disposal service and tell them it contains methacrylated monomers, oligomers and trace photoinitiator.
findings.evidence_quote: Never pour solvent that contains dissolved resin into drains or dispose of it with household waste.

findings.claim: Disposal instruction for contaminated paper towels and gloves: expose to sunlight or UV to cure the liquid resin, then household waste (Formlabs).
findings.evidence_quote: To dispose of paper towels or other supplies that have come into contact with liquid resin, expose them to sunlight or UV light to cure the liquid resin and then dispose of them with household waste.

findings.claim: Cured resin and cleaned parts cannot be recycled according to Formlabs, which tells users to discard them as household waste. This is the manufacturer's statement for its own resins.
findings.evidence_quote: Cleaned parts and cured resin cannot be recycled.

findings.claim: As supplied, the Nylon 11 powder is not RCRA hazardous waste per its SDS; the SDS section 12 says 'No data available' for persistence and degradability, so no biodegradability claim is supported.
findings.value: not hazardous waste; degradability: no data
findings.evidence_quote: As supplied, this material is not considered a hazardous waste under RCRA.

findings.claim: Unsintered used powder must be disposed of according to local ordinances for plastic waste; vacuum bags and filters count as unsintered powder waste; sintered powder and cleaned parts go to household waste and 'cannot be recycled'; empty powder cartridges and build chambers cannot be recycled.
findings.evidence_quote: Cleaned parts and sintered powder cannot be recycled.

findings.claim: Unsintered powder disposal: 'Unsintered used powder must be disposed of in accordance with your local ordinances and environmental regulations for plastic waste.'
findings.evidence_quote: Unsintered used powder must be disposed of in accordance with your local ordinances and environmental regulations for plastic waste.

findings.claim: Resin packaging: Formlabs reports its Form 4 cartridge uses 66 % less plastic than earlier designs; that is a packaging statement from the company, not an LCA of the resin.
findings.evidence_quote: The next-generation resin cartridge for Form 4 Series 3D printers uses 66% less plastic than precious designs while still delivering one full liter of material.

findings.claim: Pulverised nylon powder is a combustion risk: Formlabs requires a grounded, bonded Class II Division 2 vacuum for cleaning, no ignition sources, care to avoid dust plumes. The Nylon 11 and 12 SDS classify the powder 'Combustible Dust' (signal word Warning).
findings.evidence_quote: Pulverized plastic powder (e.g., nylon PA12) poses a combustion risk if not properly handled.

findings.claim: SDS classification of the Formlabs nylon powders: Nylon 11 and Nylon 12 are 'Combustible Dust' only; TPU 90A states no hazardous substances. Nylon 12 contains carbon black at 0.1-0.999 % (CAS 1333-86-4).
findings.value: Nylon 11/12: combustible dust only; Nylon 12: carbon black <1 %
findings.evidence_quote: Combustible Dust

findings.claim: TPU 90A powder SDS: 'There are no substances or mixtures present which are classified as hazardous.'
findings.evidence_quote: There are no substances or mixtures present which are classified as hazardous.

findings.claim: Two Formlabs documents differ in tone on powder PPE. A Formlabs-commissioned study at its own Somerville SLS lab found airborne powder below 2 % of the OSHA limit and says no special PPE, respirators or goggles are required there. The support article for customers recommends a NIOSH respirator if local exhaust does not keep particulates below the ACGIH limit or irritation occurs, plus nitrile gloves and glasses. A studio should follow the stricter one.
findings.value: <2 % of OSHA PEL at Formlabs lab (vendor study)
findings.evidence_quote: no special personal protective equipment, respirators, or goggles are required at Formlabs facilities for operating the Fuse ecosystem.

findings.claim: Customer-facing powder guidance: wear a fitted NIOSH respirator if local exhaust does not hold particulate below the ACGIH TLV or if irritation occurs.
findings.evidence_quote: Wear a properly fitted respirator approved by NIOSH if local exhaust does not keep the particulate concentration below ACGIH Threshold Limit Value or irritation occurs.

findings.claim: Fuse 1+ 30W with nitrogen: if nitrogen escapes and displaces room oxygen it becomes a hazard (OSHA: below 19.5 % oxygen is immediately dangerous to life or health); Formlabs says install an oxygen monitor with alarm in the room. Relevant because Formlabs strongly recommends inert printing for Nylon 11.
findings.value: O2 monitor needed with nitrogen; <19.5 % O2 dangerous
findings.evidence_quote: If nitrogen gas is released into the room containing the Fuse 1+ 30W and displaces the existing oxygen content there (roughly 21%), it may create a significant hazardous situation.

findings.claim: Keep humidity at or below 50 % RH around the Fuse, Fuse Sift and powder storage; unsintered powder has no defined shelf life when stored sealed, cool and dry.
findings.evidence_quote: keep the relative humidity of the environment around the printer, the Fuse Sift and other post-processing tools, and anywhere unsintered powder is stored to 50% or less at all times

findings.claim: Skin-contact use changes the wash recipe: for Tough 1500 V1/V1.1, Formlabs says parts for skin contact 'must be washed with >=99 % IPA in a Form Wash/Form Wash L for 20 minutes' (the standard recipe is 10 + 10 min), and thick walls may need longer drying before post-cure because of IPA pooling. A visitor-touchable part needs the documented skin-contact workflow, not the quick one.
findings.evidence_quote: parts must be washed with ≥99% IPA in a Form Wash/Form Wash L for 20 minutes

findings.claim: Silicone 40A solvent hazard to the equipment: a Form Wash bucket used with n-butyl acetate must not be switched back to pure IPA because it 'risks compromising the integrity of the bucket plastic'; cracking or crazing means stop use and call Formlabs.
findings.value: dedicated n-butyl acetate bucket; crazing risk
findings.evidence_quote: Once a Form Wash bucket has been used with n-Butyl Acetate, do not switch to pure IPA.

findings.claim: Formlabs recommends a 30 % refresh rate for Nylon 11 on the Fuse 1+ 30W in inert (nitrogen) atmosphere and 50 % in air: i.e. 70 % or 50 % of each build is previously used unsintered powder. Printing in air gives 'decreased and less consistent mechanical properties'.
findings.evidence_quote: Formlabs recommends a 30% refresh rate for Nylon 11, allowing for maximum reuse of materials and optimal print success.

findings.claim: In air the Nylon 11 refresh rate rises to 50 %: reuse falls to 50 % per build.
findings.evidence_quote: If you must print Nylon 11 on a Fuse 1 or Fuse 1+ 30W in an air atmosphere, use a refresh rate of 50% to maximize efficiency and printing reliability.

findings.claim: Formlabs' product pages call reused unsintered powder 'recycled powder' (Nylon 12: 'up to 70 % recycled powder'; TPU 90A: 20 % refresh = 80 % recycled). This is in-process reuse of powder that was not fused, not post-consumer recycling. The printed parts and sintered cake are not recycled by Formlabs (see disposal).
findings.evidence_quote: Get the most out of your material by printing with up to 70% recycled powder.

findings.claim: TPU 90A powder: 'A low 20% refresh rate allows you to print with 80% recycled powder for minimal waste.'
findings.evidence_quote: A low 20% refresh rate allows you to print with 80% recycled powder for minimal waste.

findings.claim: Arkema's own PA11 laser-sintering powder datasheet says its 'low refreshing factor (typically 50%)'. This is a different supplier document and a different machine ecosystem from Formlabs; it agrees with Formlabs' 50 % for air printing.
findings.evidence_quote: its low refreshing factor (typically 50%)

findings.claim: A peer-reviewed life-cycle study of recycling SLS PA12 waste powder into an injection-moulded part shows the answer depends on how waste burden is allocated: the recycled-PA12 clip's global warming potential is up to 26 % lower than PA66 under cut-off but up to 68 % higher under mass-based allocation; for the SLS part itself recycling powder cuts GWP 42 % (mass-based), and 8 % from a two-part system view. This is PA12 (EOS-type SLS), not a Formlabs-specific LCA.
findings.value: -26 % to +68 % vs PA66; -42 % / -8 % for SLS part
findings.evidence_quote: For the SLS part, recycling PA12 powder provides a 42% reduction to its life cycle GWP (mass-based allocation).

findings.claim: Fraunhofer IPA says plainly that 'a comprehensive assessment of the environmental impact of plastic-based 3D printing and the potential for greenhouse gas savings is lacking', and its project page for PA11 and PA12 powder reports no per-kilogram carbon figure.
findings.value: no per-kg GWP published on the page
findings.evidence_quote: However, a comprehensive assessment of the environmental impact of plastic-based 3D printing and the potential for greenhouse gas savings is lacking.

findings.claim: No published life-cycle assessment or carbon footprint for any Formlabs resin, powder or printer was found. Formlabs' sustainability blog gives qualitative statements (waste reduction, local production) and the 66 % cartridge-plastic figure only.
findings.evidence_quote: In SLS 3D printing, unused powder is cleaned from parts and reused in later printing batches.

findings.claim: A 2026 critical review of polymer additive manufacturing reports desktop process energy of 24.8-85.7 kJ/cm3 for filament printing (FFF) and 10.8-21.5 kJ/cm3 for SLA, but stresses that results depend strongly on functional unit and machine state, and that post-processing and utilisation can change the lifecycle result. Process energy is not the dominant question for a one-off pavilion component.
findings.value: SLA 10.8-21.5 kJ/cm3 vs FFF 24.8-85.7 kJ/cm3 (reported ranges)
findings.evidence_quote: reported desktop values span 24.8-85.7 kJ cm-3 for FFF and 10.8-21.5 kJ cm-3 for SLA

findings.claim: The same review concludes that sustainability must be judged on retained performance, processing burden, service conditions and end-of-life, 'rather than assuming that AM, recycled content, or bio-based chemistry is inherently sustainable'.
findings.value: bio-based/recycled content is not by itself sustainable
findings.evidence_quote: rather than assuming that AM, recycled content, or bio-based chemistry is inherently sustainable

findings.claim: Conventional photopolymers (what every Formlabs resin is) form permanently crosslinked networks resistant to recycling; recyclable photopolymers with dynamic bonds are a research frontier, not a commercial Formlabs product.
findings.evidence_quote: However, conventional photopolymers form permanently crosslinked networks, which are resistant to recycling.

findings.claim: A 2026 account on bio-derived resins says current research aims at switching to biomass-derived monomers and at resins that can be 'printed, depolymerized, and re-printed in a closed-loop'. Both are goals, not available Formlabs resins.
findings.evidence_quote: enhancing material circularity such that resins can be printed, depolymerized, and re-printed in a closed-loop, circular manner

findings.claim: A 2025 perspective warns that improper disposal of 3D-printing polymer materials may add to plastic pollution, and that health effects of printer emissions are 'poorly understood'.
findings.evidence_quote: improper disposal of 3D printing polymer materials may exacerbate plastic pollution

findings.claim: Formlabs describes Nylon 11 Powder as 'bio-based' on its data sheet and product page but states no percentage, feedstock or test method on either page. Of the 64 Formlabs product pages saved earlier, only Nylon 11 Powder carries 'bio-based' (my regex over the saved pages); no resin page makes a bio-based, renewable or recyclable claim. CONFIRMS the earlier agents.
findings.evidence_quote: Nylon 11 Powder is our legacy strong, highly ductile bio-based material.

findings.claim: Same wording in the technical data sheet: 'Nylon 11 Powder is a high performance, bio-based nylon material'.
findings.evidence_quote: Nylon 11 Powder is a high performance, bio-based nylon material for

findings.claim: The 100 % figure exists only for a different supplier document: Arkema's Rilsan PA11 INVENT NAT laser-sintering powder is 'a natural Polyamide 11 powder made from 100% renewable source (castor oil)' with bio-based carbon content 100 % by ASTM D6866. Formlabs does not name its Nylon 11 supplier or grade in the pages I read, so 100 % cannot be transferred to Formlabs Nylon 11. (The PDF text extractor scrambles the table labels; the value 100 % sits in the row labelled bio-based carbon content, confirmed against a search-snippet of the same sheet.)
findings.evidence_quote: is a natural Polyamide 11 powder made from 100% renewable source (castor oil)

findings.claim: ASTM D6866 measures the fraction of carbon from recent biomass (radiocarbon), not mass fraction, not biodegradability, not lower carbon footprint. So 'bio-based carbon' is the only defensible form; 'biodegradable', 'compostable', 'carbon neutral' or '100 % natural' are not supported for Nylon 11 parts. The Formlabs Nylon 11 SDS says persistence and degradability: no data available. (Interpretation, my reading; D6866 definition from background knowledge, labelled unverified background.)
findings.evidence_quote: Polyundecanamide <100

findings.claim: The Formlabs Nylon 11 SDS lists a single ingredient, polyundecanamide (CAS 25587-80-8) at '<100' %, so additive or pigment content is not itemised; any bio-based percentage for the finished Formlabs powder is therefore unknown.
findings.evidence_quote: Polyundecanamide <100

findings.claim: A 2026 review of fully bio-based vat-photopolymerisation resins says such resins are still being developed, that reactive diluents add VOC problems, and offers bio-based photoinitiators as an alternative to 'highly hazardous and toxic commercial photoinitiators, such as BAPO and TPO'. No Formlabs resin should be called bio-based on this evidence.
findings.value: fully bio-based vat resins = research; BAPO/TPO hazardous
findings.evidence_quote: an alternative to the highly hazardous and toxic commercial photoinitiators, such as BAPO and TPO, which pose serious health hazards

findings.claim: TPO photoinitiator (CAS 75980-60-8) is classified CMR category 1B reproductive toxicant in the EU by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/197, applying from 1 September 2025, and was thereby banned in cosmetics (Regulation (EU) 2025/877). None of the 18 Formlabs SDS read names TPO: BAPO is named in Flexible 80A V2, Flexible 50A (EU sheet) and Tough 1000; TPO-L (a different substance) in Grey V5, Silicone 40A and Tough 1500 V2; other resins only say 'Photoinitiator(s)', trade secret. A client or regulator asking 'is there TPO in it' cannot be answered from public sheets.
findings.value: TPO Repr. 1B from 2025-09-01; photoinitiator identity mostly undisclosed
findings.evidence_quote: TPO was classified as a CMR category 1B reproductive toxicant by Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/197 under the CLP Regulation

findings.claim: EU Directive 2024/825 lists 'biodegradable' and 'biobased' among examples of generic environmental claims that are prohibited unless recognised excellent environmental performance can be demonstrated. Member States had to apply it from 27 September 2026, already in force today (2026-11-12) in transposing states. It restricts how a trader markets to consumers; whether a B2B architectural commission is caught depends on national transposition, which I did not verify.
findings.evidence_quote: ‘biodegradable’, ‘biobased’ or similar statements that suggest or create the impression of excellent environmental performance.

findings.claim: The same Directive requires Member States to apply the measures 'from 27 September 2026'.
findings.evidence_quote: They shall apply those measures from 27 September 2026.

findings.claim: The Directive also bans presenting a claim about the whole product when it concerns only one aspect: an example is 'made with recycled material' when only the packaging is. For Formlabs Nylon 11, 'bio-based' on the powder does not license 'bio-based pavilion' if the part carries pigment, dye, coating, steel or other materials.
findings.evidence_quote: making an environmental claim about the entire product or the trader’s entire business when it actually concerns only a certain aspect of the product

findings.claim: Mamou-Mani is UK-based; the EU Directive does not apply there directly. UK guidance (CMA Green Claims Code) says 'broader, more general or absolute claims are much more likely to be inaccurate and to mislead' and requires substantiation. Both regimes point the same way: specific, evidenced, narrow claims only.
findings.evidence_quote: Broader, more general or absolute claims are much more likely to be inaccurate and to mislead.

findings.claim: The practice's own PLA carbon claims already disagree across its statements (68 %, 80 %, 73.7 % computed from the Aurora LCA, 75.5-83.7 % computed from Altostrata), and none is an independent LCA. Any Formlabs-based claim will meet that audience's habit of quoting percentages, so every number we give must trace to a sheet. (Project record, bm-mamou-mani-portfolio.json.)
findings.evidence_quote: sources disagree and none is an independent LCA

findings.claim: Naming: Formlabs' wash table says 'Flexible 50 A Resin (formerly Elastic 50 A Resin V2)'. Earlier project files use 'Elastic 50A V2' for the 39.2 % IPA uptake row; it is the same product as today's Flexible 50A, whose current SDS is dated 2026-05-29.
findings.evidence_quote: Flexible 50 A Resin (formerly Elastic 50 A Resin V2)

findings.claim: Project record: Elastic 50A V2 takes up 39.2 % isopropanol by mass in 24 h (and 0.7 % water); this confirms the earlier claim, and the new consequence is that IPA washing, not humidity, is the dominant solvent exposure for this resin during manufacture.

key_claims.claim: Every Formlabs SLA resin SDS read (14 products) classifies the liquid resin as a skin sensitiser (H317); Rigid 10K and Silicone 40A have H317 alone, while Durable V2 and High Temp V2 are also reproductive toxicants category 1B (H360) and Flexible 80A V2 and High Temp V2 cause serious eye damage (H318). Gloves, goggles and a sensitiser-aware workflow are therefore non-negotiable in lab and studio, and the two H360 resins should be excluded from a public-facing proof of concept.
key_claims.source: https://media.formlabs.com/m/3cc2feae0929233/original/-ENUS-Safety-Data-Sheet-Rigid-10K-Resin.pdf (and the 17 other SDS PDFs in the table)
key_claims.evidence_quote: H317 May cause an allergic skin reaction

key_claims.claim: Formlabs states that cleaned parts and cured resin cannot be recycled, that sintered powder and parts cannot be recycled, and that liquid resin and resin-laden IPA are potential hazardous waste. So nothing printed on a Formlabs machine may be called recyclable by the practice.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Cleaned parts and cured resin cannot be recycled.

key_claims.claim: Formlabs calls Nylon 11 Powder 'bio-based' without any percentage or supplier; the only 100 % bio-based carbon (ASTM D6866, castor oil) figure found is on Arkema's own Rilsan PA11 INVENT NAT sheet and cannot be transferred. Bio-based carbon also says nothing about biodegradability or footprint.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Nylon 11 Powder is our legacy strong, highly ductile bio-based material.

key_claims.claim: Under EU Directive 2024/825 (applies from 27 September 2026) 'biobased' and 'biodegradable' are named examples of generic environmental claims that are prohibited unless recognised excellent environmental performance can be shown; UK guidance is similar in spirit. An architecture client should be given specific, sourced statements only.
key_claims.evidence_quote: ‘biodegradable’, ‘biobased’ or similar statements that suggest or create the impression of excellent environmental performance.

recommendations: Use Rigid 10K (passive layer) and Silicone 40A or Flexible 80A V2 (active layer) only with nitrile or neoprene gloves, splash goggles (Flexible 80A V2 is H318), long sleeves, and a room with at least 3 air changes per hour; keep the vat lid closed when not printing and store finished parts 4 weeks in a ventilated place before they go near visitors.

Exclude Durable V2 and High Temp V2 (H360, reproductive toxicity 1B) from a public-facing proof of concept and ask staff who are or may become pregnant not to handle them; ask Formlabs (sds@formlabs.com) which ingredient triggers H360 and whether TPO is present in any resin we use.

Fix the wash recipe per resin before printing: Flexible 50A at most 20 min (swells about 39 % in IPA), Silicone 40A in a dedicated 80/20 IPA to n-butyl acetate bucket, High Temp at most 6 min; dry parts at least 30 min before post-cure; keep IPA in sealed labelled containers away from ignition sources.

Plan disposal on day one: a chemical-waste contract (or the sunlight-cure route for small amounts), used IPA to a waste service, cured parts and powder cake to general waste; do not promise take-back or recycling.

Water-cycling hygromorph parts should be extracted or tested before outdoor exposure: run a leachate test (soak 24 h in water, analyse for photoinitiator) and consider a barrier coating; the zebrafish work shows the hazard class, not our resin's number.

Publish only narrow, sourced environmental statements. Allowed: 'made from Nylon 11 powder which the maker describes as bio-based (percentage not stated)'; '30-50 % of unfused powder is reused'. Not allowed: recyclable, biodegradable, compostable, eco-friendly, sustainable, low-VOC, GREENGUARD, non-toxic, skin-safe (except Silicone 40A/Tough 1500 V2 within the documented workflow), carbon-negative or any percentage saving without an LCA.

If a bio-based percentage is wanted, request from Formlabs the supplier and a D6866 certificate for its Nylon 11 lot, or run our own radiocarbon test; if a real LCA is wanted, commission one (ISO 14040/44) with stated allocation, because published PA12 results swing from -26 % to +68 %.

could_not_find: The identity of the ingredient causing H360 in Durable V2 and High Temp V2: the SDS name only 'Acrylated Monomer(s)' etc. as trade secret. Needs a request to Formlabs.

Which photoinitiator (TPO, TPO-L, BAPO, other) is in Rigid 10K, Flexible 80A V2 (BAPO is named), Clear V5, Durable, High Temp and others: most SDS say only 'Photoinitiator(s)'. TPO status of any Formlabs resin unknown.

Any leachate or extractables data (water, sweat, rain) for a named Formlabs resin: the zebrafish and other work uses unnamed SLA plastic. No measured photoinitiator release from Flexible 80A V2, Rigid 10K or Silicone 40A.

Measured VOC emission rates for the Form 4 (LED, 405 nm) with any Form 4 resin: published chambers studies used Form 2 or other brands; Formlabs' own GREENGUARD data is for Alpha resins on Form Studio 1.
A glove breakthrough time for nitrile against the actual Formlabs resin mixtures or for monofunctional methacrylates; only a 1992 study on multifunctional acrylates was found.
Any life-cycle assessment or carbon footprint for a Formlabs resin, powder or printer; Fraunhofer IPA's PA11/PA12 project page gives no numbers.
The supplier and bio-based carbon percentage of Formlabs Nylon 11 Powder; no ASTM D6866 certificate; and no biodegradation data for PA11 (SDS: no data available).
A single authoritative waste code (EU List of Waste, UK) for cured and uncured Formlabs resin and for IPA-resin mixtures; Formlabs defers to local rules. I did not look up national codes.

Whether Directive 2024/825 has been transposed in the UK or in the EU states relevant to a given client, and whether a B2B architectural claim is caught; I read only the Directive text and the UK CMA Green Claims Code guidance, not national laws.
ISO 16620 or EN 16785 bio-based content certification for any Formlabs product: not found.

The Oskui 2016 Environ Sci Technol Lett paper (10.1021/acs.estlett.5b00249; DOI resolves on Crossref) was not read: no abstract in Crossref or PubMed, so it is not used. Zhu et al. (seven resins, algae and fish mortality) was seen only second-hand in a citing paper and is not used.

The PDF text of the Rigid 10K and Silicone 40A TDS ISO/biocompatibility and wash tables is extracted with pdftotext; column order can scramble, so numbers from the Arkema table (the 100 % value sits under the wrong label in the raw text) were cross-checked against the sheet's own intro sentence and a search snippet only.
Heavy local commands were not needed: C: free space was about 0.3 GB (below the 1 GB limit), so nothing was written on C:; all downloads (about 3 MB) went to D:.
